planting.note: Set divisions or nursery transplants in rich, humus-heavy woodland soil in dappled to full shade; mulch with leaf litter and keep evenly moist through the first season.

directions: A coarse, upright member of the honeysuckle family found in rich eastern hardwood forests from the upper Midwest into the Northeast, this plant produces small, dull maroon-brown tubular flowers clustered in the leaf axils each May and June that are easy to overlook but are worked by bumblebees. Its real show comes later, when clusters of bright orange-red fleshy fruits ripen along the stem and persist into fall, offering forage for small mammals and some birds. It thrives in the rich, undisturbed loam of mature woodlots and wooded ravines and pairs well with other tall woodland forbs along a shaded border where its bold, hairy foliage adds texture. Give it consistent moisture and leaf-litter mulch rather than clipped garden soil, since it resents drying out between waterings.

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions in loamy, leaf-mold-rich woodland soil in part shade; fall planting lets seed stratify naturally over winter for spring germination.

directions: This early-to-mid spring wildflower of rich Midwestern and eastern woodlands carries glossy, inch-wide yellow flowers on sprawling, bristly-haired stems for about a month, providing nectar for some of the season's first bees and flies. It is at home in the loamy, leaf-strewn floor of mesic deciduous woods, including seasonally damp swales and streambank edges where moisture lingers into early summer. The trifoliate leaves sprawl low and spread modestly, making it a good small-scale filler among sedges and spring ephemerals rather than a focal specimen. It tolerates drier shade once established but flowers best where humus is deep and moisture is dependable in spring.

planting.note: Seed needs a cold-moist stratification period, so sow in fall or cold-stratify indoors; set out in sharply drained sandy or gravelly soil on an oak savanna-like site with light shade.

directions: A true upper-Midwest regional specialty, this rare perennial sends up a dense, fuzzy spike of small creamy-white to pale yellow flowers in April before its basal rosette of leaves is fully expanded, making it one of the earliest bloomers on the oak savanna floor. It is restricted to a handful of states around the western Great Lakes, where it grows on well-drained sandy or gravelly soils in dry-mesic woodland, oak savanna, and dry prairie edges that historically burned often enough to keep the canopy open. Because it depends on that open, lightly shaded savanna structure, it declines where woodlands grow too dense or too shaded from lack of fire or brush management. In a garden setting it wants excellent drainage and a lean, sandy soil rather than rich, moisture-retentive beds, and it is best sourced as nursery-propagated seed or plants given its threatened status in the wild.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in part shade to full shade; established plants self-sow readily under trees.

directions: This quiet summer-blooming native of eastern and Midwestern deciduous forests sends up slender spikes of small pink-and-white two-lipped flowers from June into August, visited chiefly by small bees. Its common name comes from its most distinctive trait: as each flower fades, the seed capsule bends sharply downward against the stem, so a mature spike looks studded with tiny hanging pegs rather than an upright raceme. It favors the medium-moist floor of mature hardwood woods and shaded woodland edges across the upper Midwest and Great Lakes states, spreading gradually by seed once established. Because it is subtle rather than showy, it works best as a textural filler in a naturalistic shade planting alongside ferns and sedges rather than as a specimen plant.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant into moist to wet loamy soil at a woodland edge or thicket margin in part sun to light shade; tolerates seasonal wetness.

directions: A modest, easy-to-grow member of the rose family common to the upper Midwest and Northeast, this plant produces small five-petaled white flowers from late spring into midsummer, followed by bristly, hook-spined seed heads that cling to fur and clothing for dispersal. It occupies damp ground at the margins of woods, thickets, floodplains, and shaded seeps, and tolerates both brief flooding and the lower light of a half-shaded site better than most garden perennials. Its unassuming flowers draw small bees and flies, and the plant is best used as a transitional filler between a wet meadow and the woodland edge rather than as a border feature. Give it reliably moist, loamy soil and some afternoon shade and it will self-sow modestly without becoming aggressive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in mesic to wet-mesic woodland soil over calcareous bedrock if possible, in a lightly shaded canopy opening or forest edge rather than deep shade.

directions: A true Great Lakes regional endemic found in only a handful of states, this late-season aster produces white ray flowers that age to a soft lilac or rosy pink from August into October, well after most spring woodland bloomers have finished. It grows naturally in mesic to wet-mesic hardwood forests over dolomite or other calcium-rich bedrock, typically near lakes, streams, or rocky slopes, and is considered shade-intolerant despite its woodland setting — it needs the broken light of a canopy gap, forest edge, or trail margin rather than deep shade. Its heart-shaped lower leaves and branching, forked flower stems give it a lacy, airy habit that stands out among the coarser asters of fall. Because it is a species of conservation concern across its range, it is best grown from nursery-propagated stock and placed where dappled light and steady moisture mimic its narrow native habitat.
